items.title: Organization of neuropeptide signaling: cross-species insights from small model organisms
items.author: Meet Zandawala, Alessandro Filosa, Isabel Beets
items.content: <article>Neuropeptides are ancient signaling molecules that modulate neural circuit function and behavior across the animal kingdom. Model organisms such as Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and zebrafish serve as powerful in vivo models for deciphering the organization of neuropeptidergic signaling, owing to their smaller nervous systems, genetic tractability, and the growing availability of neural connectomes. In this article, we review how these organisms have advanced current understanding of neuropeptidergic transmission across three interconnected themes: (i) the roles of peptides in sensory–motor transformations, (ii) the conservation and divergence of peptidergic expression and network architecture across species, and (iii) the diversity of neurotransmission strategies employed by single neurons. Finally, we highlight recent technological innovations as well as open questions that could shape this field in the coming years.</article>

items.title: Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and phenotypic plasticity
items.author: Yonghui Zhang, Zhixin Ye, Ying Wang, Siying Tang, Gang Chen
items.content: <article>The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for therapeutic translation.</article>

items.title: An insular–orbitofrontal pathway supporting awareness of respiratory effort
items.author: Valentina Jelinčić, Andreas von Leupoldt
items.content: <article>In a recent study using human intracranial EEG recordings during inspiratory loading, Assi and colleagues identified parallel pathways for respiratory compensation and awareness. The anterior insula signals a neuromechanical mismatch to the orbitofrontal cortex for conscious appraisal, while high-frequency insular-frontal coupling enables ventilatory adjustments. The findings are highly relevant for disorders of altered respiratory perception.</article>

items.title: Apolipoprotein E4 and immune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease: mechanisms and therapeutic implications
items.author: Hao Shi, Yang Zhao, Wei Zhu, Yan-Jiang Wang, Xian-Le Bu
items.content: <article>Emerging evidence suggests that apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) functions as an organizer of brain–periphery immune crosstalk, coupling maladaptive microglial states with peripheral immune remodeling to establish a self-reinforcing neuroimmune loop that may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer’s disease. In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. In addition, APOE4 erodes the separation between central and peripheral immune compartments, enabling bidirectional immune crosstalk that amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. In this review, we synthesize evidence for APOE4-driven central and peripheral immune dysregulation; discuss therapeutic opportunities for targeting the APOE4 immune axis; and highlight the need for human-derived, longitudinal, cross-tissue studies to identify causal, stage-specific, and targetable immune nodes for precision intervention.</article>

items.title: Resilience and vulnerability in the midbrain dopamine system during aging
items.author: Gary McMurtrie, Samuel J. Mabry, Jill R. Glausier, Emily M. Rocha, Zachary Freyberg
items.content: <article>The midbrain dopamine system is integral to movement, reward, and motivation, and its dysfunction underlies a range of brain disorders. Age is a primary risk factor for many of these disorders, yet systematic analysis of how the dopamine system changes during healthy aging remains relatively understudied. In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. Elucidating these neuroadaptive mechanisms could offer a path toward preserving dopamine neuron function across the lifespan and potentially preventing age-related neurodegeneration.</article>

items.title: A brain circuit linking sleep loss to pain
items.author: Miao Li, Guang Yang
items.content: <article>Sleep loss heightens pain sensitivity, but the brain circuits involved remain unclear. In a recent study, Huang, Wang, Jiao, and colleagues identified a pathway connecting the retrosplenial cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and zona incerta that contributes to heightened sensitivity to mechanical stimulation and heat after sleep deprivation in male mice.</article>

items.title: The mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome in aging and brain diseases
items.author: Abd-El-Monsif A. Shawky, Hui-Ting Huang, Dhruv Parikh, Kahlilia C. Morris-Blanco
items.content: <article>The mitochondrial genome is a dynamic regulatory platform that extends far beyond its protein-coding capacity. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) harbors epigenetic modifications and produces diverse noncoding RNAs that influence mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis. Evidence from animal models and human studies indicates that mtDNA methylation, mitochondrial-encoded noncoding RNAs, and cytosolic release of mitochondrial nucleic acids regulate transcription, metabolism, and stress signaling. Furthermore, these mechanisms are altered in aging, neurodegenerative disease, and acute brain injury. In this review, we synthesize emerging insights into how the mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome shape mitochondrial function and serve as regulatory interfaces linking cellular stress and neuronal vulnerability in brain aging and disease.</article>

items.title: Sleep-dependent microglial functions in Alzheimer’s disease
items.author: Sara Calafate, Renzo Mancuso
items.content: <article>Sleep is a fundamental regulator of brain homeostasis, yet how distinct brain cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, actively regulate neuroinflammatory tone, metabolic waste clearance, and synaptic remodeling, thereby contributing to neural circuit maintenance and proteostasis. Delineating the different functions played by microglia during specific brain states, such as sleep, represents an active area of research. In this article, we review a growing literature supporting the notion that sleep dynamically shapes microglial functional outputs. We further suggest that the failure of the sleep–microglia axis may represent an important component of the molecular framework of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), contributing to disease progression. Finally, we discuss preclinical and clinical evidence suggesting that sleep-targeting interventions may modulate AD pathology, and highlight the possibility that restoring sleep physiology could recalibrate microglial homeostatic functions and slow disease progression.</article>

items.title: On the nature of GABAB receptors and their plasticity in the mammalian brain
items.author: Sam A. Booker
items.content: <article>Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian CNS, essential for circuit function and behaviour. In the brain, GABA activates GABAA and GABAB receptors to modulate circuit activity on behaviourally relevant timescales. GABAB receptor signalling in pre- and postsynaptic domains of neurons is often overlooked, despite the strong inhibition it produces. Importantly, GABAB receptors are diversely phosphorylated and interact with various auxiliary subunits to modify function. This review compares the evidence for the expression and modulation of GABAB receptors, their effectors, and regulatory mechanisms between cell types, brain areas, and mammalian species, particularly focusing on the plasticity of these mechanisms and their relationship to neurological diseases such as epilepsy and dementia.</article>

items.title: Interpersonal neural synchrony: one label, many phenomena
items.author: Giacomo Novembre, Atesh Koul, Félix Bigand
items.content: <article>Brains synchronize interpersonally during social interaction, yet the term ‘synchrony’ is often used to describe phenomena with different origins and functional implications. In this article, we briefly synthesize and organize these phenomena according to their signal and coupling properties, highlighting the value of disambiguation for reproducibility, theoretical clarity, and translational impact.</article>

items.title: A microglial circadian clock sculpts synapses during neurodevelopment
items.author: Annemarie J. Carver, Nicole R. Zürcher, Evan A. Bordt
items.content: <article>In a recent study, Routh and colleagues demonstrated that the circadian clock regulates microglia-directed synaptic refinement during a critical period of neurodevelopment in mice, in a sex-dependent manner. Loss of the major circadian rhythm regulator, Bmal1, in microglia induced a proinflammatory state and excessive pruning of synapses, primarily in adolescent male mice.</article>
